chunks: And from him, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Abu Abdillah, from Al-Hasan ibn Al-Husayn Al-Tabari, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Ja'far, from his father, upon them be peace, who said:

A man proposed marriage to a people, and they asked him, 'What is your trade?' He said, 'I sell animals (dawabb).' So they married him to their daughter. But then it turned out he was selling 'sananir' (a specific type of animal or beast), so they went to Ali (peace be upon him) and he validated his marriage, saying, 'Indeed, the sananir are animals.'

key_terms.الدَّوَابَّ: Animals (plural of dawabah, referring to beasts of burden or livestock)
key_terms.السَّنَانِيرَ: Sananir (a specific type of animal/beast, contextually debated but treated as a subset of dawabb here)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on marriage if the suitor's specific trade differs slightly from his general claim?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the principle of *al-umum wa al-khass* (generality and specificity) in marital contracts, where Imam Ali (AS) validated the marriage by ruling that 'sananir' (often identified as donkeys or specific camels) falls under the general category of 'animals' (*dawabb*). This ruling highlights the Shia jurisprudential approach to avoiding excessive technicality in social transactions, ensuring that a general claim suffices unless a specific defect is concealed. It serves as a foundational precedent for evaluating deception (*tadlis*) in marriage, emphasizing that the suitor's statement was not misleading enough to invalidate the union.
